title: THE WOMAN WHO MADE HANNAH CRY: WHEN THE PEOPLE CLOSEST TO YOU KNOW EXACTLY WHERE TO HURT YOU
paragraphs: THE WOMAN WHO MADE HANNAH CRY: WHEN THE PEOPLE CLOSEST TO YOU KNOW EXACTLY WHERE TO HURT YOU
What Hannah and Peninnah teach us about jealousy, unanswered prayer, family wounds, cruel comparison—and the God who can write redemption in the very place where you thought your story was ruined.
Some wounds come from enemies.
Those are painful.
But there is another kind of wound that seems to travel deeper because it comes from someone sitting at the same table.
Someone who knows your weakness.
Someone who has watched you pray.
Someone who knows what you desperately want but still do not have.
Someone who does not need to invent a lie about you because the truth of your pain is already enough ammunition.
That was Hannah's world.
And maybe, in a way you have never admitted aloud, it has been yours too.
Before you finish this article, you may recognize Hannah.
You may recognize Peninnah.
More unsettlingly, you may recognize a little of both women inside your own heart.
Because 1 Samuel does not introduce Hannah in a peaceful home where everyone understands each other. It introduces us to a complicated household.
Elkanah had two wives.
One was Hannah.
The other was Peninnah.
Then Scripture gives us one devastating contrast:
Peninnah had children.
Hannah did not.
In Hebrew, Hannah's name is written חַנָּה — Ḥannah, associated with grace or favor.
Yet the woman whose very name carried the sound of grace was living through circumstances that did not feel gracious at all.
Have you ever experienced that contradiction?
You know God is good, but your life hurts.
You believe He hears prayer, but the answer has not come.
You worship Him while secretly wondering why somebody else received the thing you have begged Him for.
You congratulate people while something inside you breaks.
You smile at another pregnancy announcement while carrying infertility.
You applaud another wedding while wondering whether you will ever be chosen.
You celebrate someone else's promotion while your bills keep arriving.
You watch another family laughing together while yours barely speaks.
You see someone's children walking with God while you lie awake wondering where your own child went spiritually.
You say, "I'm happy for you."
And perhaps you really are.
But later, when nobody is watching...
you cry.
That is why Hannah's story refuses to become a shallow motivational slogan.
Scripture says Elkanah loved Hannah, yet "the LORD had closed her womb" (1 Samuel 1:5).
Those words require humility.

The biblical text does not present Hannah's infertility as proof that she lacked faith, nor does it tell us that she had committed some secret sin that caused it. Scripture simply places her suffering beneath the mysterious sovereignty of God.
That distinction matters.
Because suffering people have endured enough pain without Christians adding accusations God never made.
Not every unanswered prayer means you did something wrong.
Not every delay means your faith is defective.
Not every barren season is divine punishment.
And not every painful chapter gives us permission to pretend we understand everything God is doing.
But Hannah's empty arms were not the only thing hurting her.
There was Peninnah.
The Hebrew text describes Peninnah with the word צָרָתָהּ — tsaratah — her rival, adversary, or competing wife.
Then comes one of the most painful sentences in the chapter:
"וְכִעֲסַתָּה צָרָתָהּ גַּם־כַּעַס"
Ve-khi'asatah tsaratah gam-ka'as...
Her rival repeatedly provoked her bitterly.
The language carries the idea of vexing, provoking, causing grief or anger.
Peninnah did not accidentally stumble onto Hannah's wound.
She pressed it.
And Scripture says this happened "year by year."
Think about that.
Not once.
Not one insensitive remark everybody regretted afterward.
Not one terrible holiday.
Year...
after...
year.
Hannah knew what was coming.
The journey to worship should have been sacred, yet even there she encountered torment.
Peninnah possessed what Hannah desperately wanted, and instead of receiving her blessing with humility, she apparently weaponized it against the woman who lacked it.
There is something frighteningly contemporary about that.
Because human beings are still doing this.
We turn marriages into status symbols.
Children into trophies.
Ministry into competition.
Money into identity.
Beauty into superiority.
Education into arrogance.
Followers into validation.
Spiritual gifts into rankings.
Even testimonies can become weapons when we use what God has given us to make another wounded person feel spiritually inferior.
Sometimes the person hurting you is not miserable because she has nothing.
Sometimes she is hurting you while holding the very thing you wish you had.
And sometimes having more does not heal an insecure heart.
Peninnah had children.
Yet Hannah had Elkanah's special affection.
The text says he loved Hannah.
Perhaps somewhere inside this fractured household lived the poisonous machinery of comparison.
One woman could look across the room and think, "She has his heart."
The other could look back and think, "She has the children."
And suddenly everybody is measuring.
Everybody is noticing.
Everybody is hurting.
This is what comparison does to families.
It teaches wounded people to stare at another person's portion until they become blind to their own.
It whispers:
Why does Mom treat her differently?
Why does Dad always praise him?
Why did she get married first?
Why does his career succeed?
Why are their children doing better?
Why does everybody listen to her?
Why did God give them what He withheld from me?
Comparison can turn brothers into competitors, sisters into strangers, spouses into scorekeepers, parents into judges, and homes into emotional battlefields.
And if comparison remains unconfessed long enough, another person's blessing can begin to feel like your humiliation.
But there is something remarkable about Hannah.
We are never told that she destroyed Peninnah in return.
She cried.
She stopped eating.
She hurt deeply.
Then she went somewhere with her pain.
To God.
First Samuel 1:10 says Hannah was "bitter of soul"—מָרַת נָפֶשׁ, marat nephesh.
This is not sanitized spirituality.
Her soul hurt.
She wept bitterly.
And she prayed.
Please do not miss that order.
Hannah did not wait until she felt emotionally impressive before approaching God.
She came broken.
Her prayer was so intense and inward that Eli saw her lips moving without hearing her voice and wrongly assumed she was drunk.
Even the priest misunderstood her.
Imagine that.
Tormented at home.
Misunderstood at church.
Still praying.
Somebody reading this knows that loneliness.
You tried explaining what happened in your family, and people minimized it.
You told someone you were struggling, and they gave you a cliché.
You came to church carrying something almost unbearable, and everyone around you saw your clothes but not your battle.
You worshipped while exhausted.
You sang while grieving.
You smiled while unraveling.
And perhaps you wondered:
Does anybody actually see me?
God did.
Hannah told Eli:
"I have been pouring out my soul before the LORD."
The Hebrew imagery is powerful.
שָׁפַכְתִּי אֶת־נַפְשִׁי לִפְנֵי יְהוָה
Shafakhti et-nafshi lifnei YHWH.
"I poured out my soul before the LORD."
Not polished it.
Not edited it.
Not disguised it.
Poured it out.
There are moments when prayer is not eloquent.
Prayer is tears falling onto a pillow.
Prayer is sitting in your car because you cannot walk inside yet.
Prayer is whispering "Jesus" because every other sentence feels impossible.
Prayer is telling God, "I don't understand."
Prayer is admitting, "I'm jealous."
"I'm angry."
"I'm tired."
"I'm scared."
"I feel forgotten."
"I don't know how much longer I can carry this."
God is not frightened by honest grief.
Biblical faith does not require pretending that pain does not hurt.
But Hannah teaches us something else.
Pain must have somewhere holy to go.
Because pain that is never surrendered can become bitterness.
And bitterness eventually looks for someone to punish.
Maybe that is part of what makes Peninnah such a warning.
We know considerably less about her inner life than we know about Hannah's, so we should resist inventing motives Scripture does not reveal.
But we do know what she did.
She provoked a hurting woman.
Repeatedly.
And that should force an uncomfortable question:
Have you become someone's Peninnah?
Not because you have two husbands or live in an ancient Israelite household.
But because you know where somebody hurts...
and sometimes you press there.
Maybe during arguments you bring up the failure your spouse already regrets.
Maybe you compare your children.
Maybe you make jokes about someone's weight, income, singleness, education, infertility, past, addiction, divorce, parenting, or mistakes.
Maybe you post things partly because you know a particular person will see them.
Maybe you call it honesty when it is actually cruelty.
Maybe you tell yourself, "I'm only telling the truth."
But truth without love can still be wielded like a knife.
Being wounded does not give us permission to wound.
Being jealous does not excuse cruelty.
Being overlooked does not authorize revenge.
And being blessed never gives us the right to humiliate someone whose prayer remains unanswered.
This is where the story becomes more than Hannah versus Peninnah.
Because if we only read Scripture asking, "Which character am I?" we can still miss the greater story.
The Bible is ultimately moving us toward Christ.
Hannah eventually conceived and gave birth to Samuel.
But Samuel was not merely Hannah's personal happy ending.
He would become a prophet and judge in Israel. He would anoint David.
And through David's royal line, Scripture moves forward toward Jesus Christ.
Do you see the breathtaking movement?
A woman crying because she could not have a child...
prays.
A child is eventually born.
That child becomes part of Israel's redemptive history.
Samuel anoints David.
And generations later, Jesus Christ comes as the promised Son of David.
Hannah could see her pain.
God could see history.
Hannah could see an empty womb.
God could see Samuel.
Hannah could see Peninnah.
God could see generations.
That does not mean every Christian will eventually receive the exact earthly thing for which they pray.
Christian hope is deeper than that.
Some prayers are answered differently than we desire.
Some losses remain losses in this life.
Some wombs remain empty.
Some marriages are not restored.
Some prodigals take years to return, and some situations remain painfully unresolved.
The Gospel is not "follow God and eventually He will give you your preferred ending."
The Gospel is infinitely greater.
God has given us His Son.
Jesus entered our broken world, bore sin at the cross, died in the place of sinners, and rose again.
Our deepest problem was never merely that life hurts.
Our deepest problem is sin separating humanity from a holy God.
And our greatest hope is not that every circumstance becomes comfortable.
Our greatest hope is Christ.
At the cross, Jesus carried what we could never carry away ourselves.
Sin.
Guilt.
Condemnation.
Our rebellion against God.
And because He rose from the dead, grace has the final word for everyone who belongs to Him.
That is why family pain does not have to become your identity.
What your father said is not your identity.
What your mother failed to give you is not your identity.
What your sibling did is not your identity.
What your former spouse called you is not your identity.
What happened behind the closed doors of your childhood home is not your identity.
Even what you yourself have done is not beyond the reach of Christ's redeeming grace when you repent and come to Him.
Maybe your family story contains scandal.
Betrayal.
Favoritism.
Jealousy.
Abandonment.
Divorce.
Addiction.
Infidelity.
Years of silence.
Manipulation.
Cruel words.
Funerals where relatives still refused to speak.
Christmas dinners where everyone pretended.
Church photographs where everybody smiled.
Secrets nobody mentions.
Jesus is not intimidated by messy family histories.
Look at the genealogy through which He entered the world.
Scripture does not airbrush human brokenness before announcing the Savior.
God brings redemption into real human history.
That is why our message remains:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by calling evil good.
Not by promising every relationship will be restored exactly as we desire.
But by refusing to allow sin, shame, bitterness, or another person's cruelty to have ultimate authority over the person Christ redeems.
And perhaps the most important question now is not:
"Who was your Peninnah?"
You probably already know.
The harder question may be:
"What are you going to do with the wound?"
Will you rehearse it until it becomes your personality?
Will you retaliate?
Will you become cruel because someone was cruel to you?
Will you spend another decade waiting for an apology before allowing yourself to live?
Or will you pour your soul before the Lord?
Forgiveness does not mean pretending abuse was acceptable.
It does not mean refusing wise boundaries.
It does not mean immediately trusting an unsafe person.
It does not erase justice or accountability.
Christian forgiveness means relinquishing personal vengeance into God's hands and refusing to let hatred become your master.
Sometimes reconciliation becomes possible.
Sometimes wisdom requires distance.
But bitterness must never become your god.
Jesus did not rescue you so the person who wounded you could continue living rent-free inside your soul.
And if, while reading this, the Holy Spirit has shown you that you have been the one doing the wounding...
do not hide behind shame.
Repent.
There is grace for Peninnah-shaped hearts too.
That may be one of the most beautiful truths in Christianity.
The Gospel is not merely good news for victims who need healing.
It is good news for guilty people who need forgiveness.
At the cross, there is mercy for the person who cried...
and mercy for the person who caused tears when that sinner genuinely repents and trusts Christ.
Maybe you need to apologize.
Maybe you need to stop comparing your children.
Maybe you need to call your sister.
Maybe you need to confess what jealousy has been turning you into.
Maybe you need to forgive without waiting for the other person to become worthy of forgiveness.
Maybe tonight you simply need to shut the door, kneel beside your bed, and finally pour out the sentence you have been afraid to say to God.
Whatever it is...
do not waste your pain by letting it teach you cruelty.
Let it drive you toward Christ.
You do not owe strangers your private story. But sometimes three honest words are enough to tell another wounded believer, "You're not the only one still fighting."
And if you know somebody who has been carrying family pain quietly, send this to them.
Not as an accusation.
As a hand on their shoulder.

Invite your family, your Christian friends, the exhausted believer, the person drifting from God, the seeker, and even the unbelieving friend who thinks Christianity has nothing meaningful to say to broken families. Let them encounter daily Scripture, biblical truth, conviction, encouragement, healing, discipleship, and the Gospel of Jesus Christ.

If you genuinely want to glorify God through supporting Gospel-centered work, don't reduce that desire merely to words. Pray. Live the Gospel. Serve your local church. Give generously where God leads. Share biblical truth.
Jesus Christ is the treasure.
No ministry replaces Him.
No merchandise makes you faithful.
No Facebook page can forgive your sins.
Christ alone saves.
Turn from sin. Trust Him. Follow Him.
And when your family story becomes painful again, remember Hannah.
Remember the woman who walked toward worship while carrying a wound.
Remember the tears.
Remember the silent moving lips.
Remember the soul poured out before God.
Remember that the chapter that made Hannah weep was not the final chapter God was writing.
And perhaps that is what somebody desperately needed to hear tonight.
The person who wounded you may have touched a chapter of your story—but only Jesus Christ has the authority to write its ending.
